rationale: The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few blink, movement or muscle bursts can dominate a mean-averaged Welch PSD. That is worst in the eyes-open condition and in frontal delta, and it skews relative band power. This version averages the Welch segments with the median (4-s windows, 50% overlap) instead of the mean, which makes each subject's spectrum robust to short transient artifacts. It should also hold up better on external recordings from a different amplifier and clinic. Everything else stays the same.

I'm splitting the five coarse bands into seven narrower ones: alpha into lower (8–10 Hz) and upper (10–13 Hz), and beta into beta1 (13–20 Hz) and beta2 (20–30 Hz). In MDD the alpha-power and beta-activity effects are reported mostly within these sub-bands, and the wide bands average them away. The features stay log-relative power, so they still don't depend on amplitude scale for the external dataset.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so eye blinks and movement bursts inflate the mean-averaged Welch PSD. That distorts the relative delta and gamma power. Switching Welch to median averaging across segments gives a robust spectral estimate that ignores sparse artifact-laden segments without explicit rejection. This should sharpen the true band-power differences between MDD and controls and transfer better to other clinics.

The recordings have no artifact rejection, so a few eye blinks or muscle bursts in a 2-minute recording can inflate frontal delta and gamma in the mean-averaged Welch spectrum. This should give cleaner relative band power for the classifier, and it should also hold up better on the external clinic's data.
